<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written with plausible examples and no fake sourcing, but B consistently won the decisive clashes. B exploited A's concession that independent central banks are democratically created and bounded, reframing delegation as democracy's own testimony that being right outranks being authorized. B's distinction between source of authority and weight in decision-making (the surgeon analogy) neutralized A's revocation argument, and B's inversion of A's Ulysses image—the rope is right and the sailor is wrong—was the sharpest single move. B also extracted and leveraged A's concession that a democratically authorized policy raising child mortality is a bad decision, showing authorization does not make decisions good. A's counter (means/ends, "rented, scoped, revocable," blunt correction beats none) was coherent and well-executed, and A answered pressure questions directly with proper A1/A2 format, but the closing "ends are competence-dependent all the way down" and "coin flip wearing a crown" left A's core frame damaged. A's clipped opening is a minor execution cost. B made the debate easier to decide and controlled the framing dispute about what "matters more in public decision-making" means.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 [B2.1]-[B2.2] seizing A's concession that central banks are "democratically created and bounded" and converting it into evidence that democracies deliberately place being-correct beyond authorization; A never fully recovered, and B's later Ulysses inversion [B4.5] and closing exploitation of the child-mortality concession [B5.4] sealed the exchange.</best_rebuttal>
